a. Agency Interpretation of Statutes
The Balance Between Courts and Agencies in Statutory 
Interpretation: A Brief Survey
It is impossible to do justice to a topic as complex as the development 
of judicial-executive balance in statutory interpretation in a single 
casebook, let alone a single chapter. The following materials are intended 
to situate the principal cases in their proper context.
Nineteenth Century Practice
Early courts controlled administrative action in one of two ways. In 
the first, a plaintiff could bring a common law damages action against an 
officer. For purposes of these lawsuits, the official was treated as a private 
party who had a special defense, his statutory authority. If the official had 
made an error of either law or fact, and the damage to the plaintiff was of 
a sort that could be remedied by a particular common law action, the official 
was hable. Save in a few special instances provided by statute, the 
reasonableness of the official’s conduct was not a defense. But even while 
exercising independent judgment in such cases, the Court accorded a type 
of weight to customary and contemporaneous interpretations of legal text, 
including statutory text. For instance, in Edwards^ Lessee v. Darby, 12 
Wheat. 206 (1827), the Court explained that “[i]n the construction of a 
doubtful and ambiguous law, the contemporaneous construction of those 
who were called upon to act under the law, and were appointed to carry its 
provisions into effect, is entitled to very great respect.”
In the other major form of judicial review, a suit for mandamus or 
injunction, courts probed the official’s authority for jurisdictional defects or 
to ensure that he had exercised his discretion in carrying out the relevant 
statutory functions. If so, the writ would not he. On the other hand, if the 
official were carrying out a merely ministerial function providing no room 
for discretion or judgment, the court would determine de novo whether the 
official had acted or failed to act in accordance with the statute. A leading
